newsitem.title: UK: Optimism on Greek prospects drives drachma deals.
newsitem.headline: Optimism on Greek prospects drives drachma deals.

text.p: A punt on Greece joining EMU in the second wave is driving a sharp increase in the supply of high-yielding Greek drachma Eurobonds, bankers said on Tuesday.
"Greece at some point will apply for monetary union and at some stage will achieve it," a Deutsche Morgan Grenfell spokesman in London said.
"If you wait until it is signed, sealed and settled you'll have missed the boat. The Greek drachma sector offers the prospect of travelling hopefully, rather than arrival," he added.

Greece (which is outside the European Union's exchange rate mechanism) is not expected to be among the first group of countries planned for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, but may well be in the second wave taking place a year or two later.
Two drachma bonds were launched on Tuesday for Ford Credit and International Finance Corp, making a combined total of 37.5 billion drachma or $129 million.

This brought the number of Eurobonds denominated in Greek drachma so far in 1997 to 13, worth a combined $700 million. In the whole of 1996 there were only five deals worth $479 million, Capital DATA Bondware showed.
Borrowers this year have included Abbey National, the EIB, GECC, IBM and the World Bank.

"People have started putting their toes back in the water as the currency stability has picked up," a dealer said. "But people will shun these markets if the risk profile looks too high or uncomfortable."

Manos Arzinos, head of bonds trading at Alpha Credit Bank in Athens, said the Greek government bonds' yield pick-up over other European paper and the stability of the drachma was attracting investors.

The 10-year Greek government bond spread over the Italian government bond (BTP) 10-year has widened from 200 basis points to 300 b.p. in around two months and it was likely the spread will tighten again, dealers said.
"We have seen more and more investors involved in the drachma sector which is encouraging," Arzinos said.
Bankers said another reason for the interest was Greek economic stability.
"The domestic progress that has been made in the management of the Greek economy has been quite considerable, leading to currency stability and lower rates of inflation," the DMG banker said.
The Czech crown and South African rand sectors are contenders for high-yielding currency demand, and the drachma offers diversification.

"Investors do not want to put all their eggs in one basket, the rand has a lot of upside and we will see a lot of activity there but it has limited capacity, like the Greek drachma market," a dealer said.
"People do not want to build up huge concentrations in one or another currency. Its the old case of you 'thirst a little you drink a little'," the DMG banker said.
There is a healthy mix of both retail and institutional European investor demand, from Germany, Switzerland, Italy and the Benelux, for high yielding currencies, dealers said.
But bankers said there was a limit to the capacity of the market.

"Its not an unlimited market, you do a couple of deals and that will occupy the market for some time," a dealer said. "The recent deals are going into pockets of identified demand, rather than a scattergun approach targeted at retail investors."
